record.title: A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
record.locator: Section II, equations (14)–(26): cancellation outside a fixed-depth local observable’s support. Background for the finite-tree explanation, not the dense-SK or large-degree transfer theorem.

aligned_passages.text: ### 8.1 Rooted realisation and the observable it preserves The fixed-depth spin–boson representation has an antecedent in [Boulebnane et al., Theorem 2 (informal), equations (10)–(11), p. 3][spin-boson]: as the degree grows with depth fixed, the symmetric tree state converges to a spin coupled to finitely many bosonic modes. The manuscript credits that representation, then proves the occupation, insertion and surrounding-circuit estimates needed below. Its additional task is to control the energy observable and substitutions inside a circuit, beyond identifying a limiting state. [OpenAI (2026b), §2][q-fock]. The immediate task is to realise the finite Gaussian spin from §7 in a space where its shifted correlation sum becomes an energy observable. We will identify that sum with a rooted quadratic form, then relate the same form to the scaled edge energy of a fixed circuit; §8.5 supplies the final transfer to SK. For an ordinary depth-$p$ word, this tree calculation uses only finitely many spins. Conjugate $Z_iZ_j$ backwards through the circuit. A mixer rotates the spins already in its support without enlarging that support. In a cost layer all edge factors commute, so factors disjoint from the current support commute past the other factors and cancel. The remaining factors enlarge support by at most one graph step. After $p$ pairs, the edge expectation therefore depends only on its radius-$p$ backward light cone. On the $(D+1)$-regular tree this contains at most $2\sum_{r=0}^pD^r$ vertices; the spins outside factor out of the product-state expectation. Thus fixed depth gives fixed tree height, although the number of children grows with $D$. This locality explains the finite tree calculation; the equality with dense SK is the separate transfer theorem in §8.5. [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann (2014), §II, equations (14)–(26)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1). On a rooted tree, factor a circuit as $U=(\bigotimes_jU_j)u$, where each $U_j$ contains operations wholly in child subtree $j$. Conjugating a root observable $P$ reduces to $u^*Pu$; its insertion vector is $u^*Pu\,\mathrm{vac}$, centered when its vacuum mean is zero. This factorization is why child operations enter the recursion below. The first change of setting preserves a specified quadratic form. At height zero the pointed space is $\mathsf k=\mathbb C^2\otimes L^2(\text{seed})$, with distinguished vector $\omega=|+\rangle\otimes1$. Recursively, $$ \mathcal H_0=\mathsf k,\qquad \mathcal H_{h+1}=\mathsf k\otimes\Gamma_s(\mathcal H_h^\circ), $$ where $\mathcal H_h^\circ$ is the orthogonal complement of the vacuum and $\Gamma_s$ is symmetric Fock space. A particle here is one child subtree whose state differs from its vacuum. It is not one physical spin. The occupation embedding identifies a symmetric state with $m$ nonvacuum children among $D$ available children with its $m$-particle vector, using the factor $\binom Dm^{-1/2}$. Adding empty descendants gives compatible embeddings between heights. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, pointed spaces and occupation embeddings][q-fock]. For a child direction $f$, write $q(f)=a^*(f)+a(f)$ and $W(f)=e^{iq(f)}$. Explicitly, $\Gamma_s(H)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}H^{\otimes_s m}$, with vacuum $\Omega$ in sector zero. On sector $m$, $a^*(f)\psi=\sqrt{m+1}\operatorname{Sym}(f\otimes\psi)$, and $a(f)$ is its adjoint. The number operator is multiplication by $m$; more generally $d\Gamma(A)$ sums $A$ over those $m$ child factors. The vacuum characteristic function $\langle\Omega,e^{itq(f)}\Omega\rangle=e^{-t^2\|f\|^2/2}$ fixes the Gaussian normalization. In the real classical sector, a centred child vector $f$ produces a parent Gaussian position $\mathsf G(f)=q(f)$ with $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle, \qquad \|[\mathsf G(f)-\mathsf G(g)]\mathrm{vac}\|=\|f-g\|. $$ The receiving root's own seed is a separate, independent tensor factor. The root shift $$ \mathsf Lf=\omega\otimes a^*(f)\Omega $$ is an isometry on centred vectors, and is extended by zero on the vacuum. Its adjoint extracts the root-vacuum, one-child component, including a constant receiving-root seed. For a classical function of orthonormal Gaussian positions, this is its first Gaussian chaos. These covariance, independence and projection properties have distinct roles in the next calculation. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, root shift and classical first chaos][q-root-energy] [OpenAI (2026b), §2, classical Gaussian positions][q-gaussian]. Start with the standard root seed $g_0=S$ and recursively set $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. Suppose $g_0,\ldots,g_{j-1}$ are centred orthonormal vectors. The covariance identity gives independent standard normals $Z_1,\ldots,Z_j$. In the scalar construction of §7, the multiplier of $Z_j$ in $g_j$ depends only on its predecessors. Conditional centring therefore makes $g_j$ orthogonal to $g_1,\ldots,g_{j-1}$, and the chosen normaliser $c_j$ gives unit norm. Independence of the receiving-root seed gives orthogonality to $g_0$. This closes the induction. Compatible height embeddings ensure that the earlier variables are the same variables when the formula is embedded at greater height. Oddness of $u$ and evenness of $a$ make $Y_j$ and $g_j$ odd under simultaneous seed reversal. The extra centred rounding variable $2F_{\rm G}(Z_{N+1})-1$ is odd as well, so $F_N$ is centred. It is independent of the receiving-root seed, hence $\langle F_N,g_0\rangle=0=A_0$. With $A_j,B_{j+1}$ as in §7, first-chaos projection gives $$ \mathsf L^*F_N=\sum_{j=0}^NB_{j+1}g_j,\qquad \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf LF_N\rangle =\sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1}. $$ Thus the construction identifies both the scalar law and the required rooted energy. The Gaussian covariance rule does not declare distinct calculations on shared descendant subtrees independent. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “A finite Gaussian formula and its rooted energy”][q-rooted-classical]. The connection to an edge observable is another statement. Let $f_D$ be centred, invariant under rooted permutations of complete child subtrees, and supported at a fixed finite radius. Suppose its occupation embedding converges strongly to $v$, with a uniformly bounded expected top-generation occupation $\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$. Put $M=D+1$ and $R_M=\sqrt{1-\mathsf N/M}$. To see the decomposition, delete the distinguished edge and project onto the vacuum on either resulting half-tree. There are four pairings. The vacuum–vacuum pairing is zero by centring. If only one side is excited, the other side forces the root and all remaining branches into their vacuum; root symmetry gives the term $M^{-1/2}\langle\mathsf L^*f_D,R_Mf_D\rangle$ or its conjugate. In the pairing where both sides are excited, each projected vector has squared norm $M^{-1}\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$ by symmetry among the $M$ branches. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds their pairing by that same quantity. Finally, deleting one vacuum child multiplies the $m$-particle sector by $\sqrt{\binom{M-1}{m}/\binom{M}{m}}=\sqrt{1-m/M}$, which identifies $R_M$. Thus the exact edge decomposition is $$ \langle f_{D,i},f_{D,j}\rangle =\frac2{\sqrt M}\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathsf L^*f_D,R_Mf_D\rangle +\varepsilon_D, \qquad |\varepsilon_D|\le\frac{\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle}{M}. $$ Vacuum deletion also gives $\|R_Mf_D-f_D\|^2\le M^{-1}\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$. Consequently, $$ \lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\sqrt D}{2} \langle f_{D,i},f_{D,j}\rangle=\mathcal E(v). $$ Strong convergence alone does not control the scaled remainder. The occupation estimate is supplied later for the relevant finite circuits. The occupation assumption cannot be dropped merely because vectors converge in norm. For orthogonal unit vectors $e_m$ in sector $m$, $\psi_k=\sqrt{1-1/k}\,\Omega+k^{-1/2}e_{k^2}$ tends to $\Omega$ in norm, whereas $\langle\psi_k,\mathsf N\psi_k\rangle=k$. The elementary continuity bound $$ |\mathcal E(v)-\mathcal E(w)| \le(\|v\|+\|w\|)\|v-w\| $$ will control every subsequent approximation after the observable has been identified. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Energy as a root shift,” including its exact finite-degree decomposition][q-root-energy]. The three identifications use different information: First, passing from the finite Gaussian formula to the rooted classical sector preserves the joint Gaussian law and the same $F_N$. This uses covariance, conditional centring and independence of the receiving-root seed. Second, the root-vacuum and first-chaos projection identify the energy itself: $\mathcal E(F_N)=S_{T,N}$. Third, for a finite-degree circuit insertion tending to $v$, root invariance, fixed radius, strong convergence and uniform occupation control imply that the scaled edge expectation tends to $\mathcal E(v)$. The first two calculations were given above. The third uses the source's edge decomposition; the requisite circuit estimates enter in §8.2.
